coredata.dc:description: Fusarium sp. FS1301, a poly(butylene succinate) (PBS)-degrading strain, was isolated by screening oil-polluted soil. In this study, the biodegradation behavior of PBS films in the presence of Fusarium sp. FS1301 was investigated. Specifically, the characteristics of PBS films before and after degradation were analyzed. Differential scanning calorimetry and scanning electron microscopy results revealed that both the amorphous and crystalline regions of PBS were degraded by Fusarium sp. FS1301. PBS depolymerase was purified from the culture supernatant of liquid mineral medium with PBS emulsion. The molecular mass of the purified enzyme was determined to be 20 kDa by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. The optimal pH and temperature for enzyme activity were 8.0 and 50 °C, respectively. PBS depolymerase maintained its activity from 20 °C to 50 °C and from pH 5.0 to 9.0. PBS depolymerase also significantly degraded poly(ε-caprolactone) but could not degrade poly(hydroxybutyrate) and poly(lactic acid). Na+ and K+ robustly promoted enzyme activity, whereas EDTA and β-mercaptoethanol significantly inhibited it. The main degradation products of PBS depolymerase were identified as 1, 4-succinate, succinate-butanediol, succinate-butanediol-succinate, and succinate-butanediol-succinate-butanediol by mass spectrometry. Furthermore, purified PBS depolymerase was found to be identical to cutinase from Fusarium solani by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry.

head.ce:title: Biodegradation of poly(butylene succinate) by Fusarium sp. FS1301 and purification and characterization of poly(butylene succinate) depolymerase

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Fusarium sp. FS1301, a poly(butylene succinate) (PBS)-degrading strain, was isolated by screening oil-polluted soil. ce:section.ce:para: Consumption of plastics synthesized using petroleum byproducts is continuously increasing, and most of such plastics cannot be degraded in the environment [1–3]. To solve this problem, biodegradable plastics are being promoted as environment-friendly substitutes. Understanding the mechanisms and optimal conditions for degradation of biodegradable plastics is, therefore, of great commercial and public health significance.

Biodegradable plastics can be degraded into H2O and CO2 in the environment; as such, these plastics do not produce “white pollution” and are environment-friendly [4–7]. Poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) is one of the most promising biodegradable aliphatic polyesters. Compared with common plastics, PBS not only has several good thermomechanical properties, but is also biodegradable and environmentally compatible [8,9]. For these reasons, PBS is widely used in the production of bottles, shopping bags, and agricultural materials [10,11].

Several studies on PBS degradability have reported the existence of PBS-degrading microorganisms. Ishii et al. found that the PBS-degrading fungus Aspergillus fumigatus degrades 80% of PBS after 30 days in soil [10]. Kitamoto et al. isolated two strains of Pseudozyma antarctica and reported that these strains degraded 60% and 20% of PBS on agar plates [12]. Uchida et al. cloned PBS depolymerase from Acidovorax delafieldii and found that PBS depolymerase showed similarities to lipases of Streptomyces and Mollaxella spp [13]. Maeda et al. purified a PBS-degrading enzyme from Aspergillus oryzae and identified the enzyme as cutinase, which degrades cutin, the waxy polymer covering the surfaces of plants [14]. These studies have shown that many microorganisms in the environment have the ability to degrade PBS. However, only a few studies have focused on the isolation of PBS-degrading strain and purification of PBS depolymerase. Therefore, isolation of PBS-degrading microorganisms, purification of the enzyme, and understanding of the degradation mechanism are of great importance.

In the present study, Fusarium sp. FS1301, a PBS-degrading strain, was isolated and found to have high degradability of PBS. The degradation behaviors of Fusarium sp. FS1301 were characterized by analyzing PBS films before and after degradation. Specifically, PBS degradation rate was calculated and degraded PBS films were characterized. Furthermore, PBS depolymerase was purified and its molecular properties were documented.
PBS was obtained from Anqing He Xing Chemical Corp. Ltd. (Anqing, China). The number-average molecular weight of PBS was 150 000 to 210 000.

The cultivation medium was a mineral medium that contained PBS emulsion (0.1%, w/v) with or without agar (2%, w/v). PBS (0.1%, w/v) was emulsified by adding Plysurf A210G (0.01%, w/v) in 10 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) [15]. The mineral medium contained MgSO4⋅7H2O (0.5 g) NH4Cl (1.0 g), CaCl2·2H2O (0.005 g), KH2PO4 (5.54 g), and Na2HPO4·12H2O (11.94 g), pH 7.0, in 1000 mL deionized water. Unless otherwise stated, all chemicals used were of analytical grade.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Isolation and identification of PBS-degrading microorganisms
ce:section.ce:para: Oil-polluted soil samples from the LiaoHe Oil Field were transferred into liquid isolation medium cultivated at 30 °C and shaken (100 rpm) for 15 days. Then, a 1 mL culture of the solid isolation medium was cultivated at 30 °C for 5 days. Clear zone-forming colonies were purified via repeated transfer onto PBS mineral agar plates. The internal transcribed spacer sequences of the strains were sequenced by Shanghai Sangon Biological Engineering Technology & Services Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China) and compared with those sequenced by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation of PBS films by PBS-degrading microorganisms
ce:section.ce:para: Fusarium sp. FS1301 was cultivated in 250 mL flasks with 100 mL of liquid mineral medium containing PBS films (30 mm × 10 mm × 0.1 mm) as the sole carbon source and shaken (100 rpm) at 30 °C. After incubation for different durations, films were carefully collected and thoroughly washed with methanol and deionized water to remove any media components or mycelium that might be present on the surface of the films. Then, they were completely vacuum dried at 50 °C until a constant weight was obtained [16]. The surfaces of the predegraded and postdegraded PBS films were observed under a scanning electron microscope (XL30 ESEM FEG; FEI Co., Netherlands) at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization of poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) degraded films
ce:section.ce:para: The thermal behaviors of predegraded and postdegraded films were investigated by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA; Pyris-1, Perkin–Elmer, Waltham, MA, USA). All scans were carried out from 100 °C to 600 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 under nitrogen atmosphere. The thermal properties of the samples were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC; Diamond, Perkin–Elmer USA). The predegraded and postdegraded films were tested by heating from 50 °C to 230 °C at a rate of 10 °C min−1 under nitrogen atmosphere.

PBS depolymerase activity was tested as follows: 1 mL of the enzyme solution was added into 3 mL of PBS emulsion and incubated at 40 °C for 20 min. An ultraviolet spectrophotometer (2600 UV-VIS; UNICO, USA) was used to test the optical density (OD630 nm) before and after incubation. One unit of PBS-degrading enzyme activity was defined as a 0.001 OD decrease in absorbance per minute at 630 nm [17].

After cultivation of Fusarium sp. FS1301 in PBS-emulsified liquid medium at 30 °C for 5 days, the culture medium was centrifuged at 18 000 × g for 10 min. Five liters of cultivated suspension were concentrated via ultrafiltration using a membrane with a molecular weight cutoff of 10 kDa. The concentrated supernatant (total volume, 750 mL) was dialyzed against 20 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) and applied into a DEAE Sepharose Fast Flow column (1 cm × 20 cm) washed with the same buffer. A linear gradient of NaCl (0 M–1 M) was applied to wash the adsorbed proteins. The collected active fractions were dialyzed against potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) and freeze dried. The freeze-dried enzyme powder was re-dissolved and applied into Sephadex G-100 (1.6 cm × 90 cm) columns. The collected active fractions were dialyzed against potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0). The purified PBS-degrading polymerase was combined and kept at −80 °C. All steps were performed at 4 °C.

The purified enzyme was separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) using a 12% gel. The gel was stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue R-250 to locate the protein bands. A low molecular weight marker (Pharmacia Co., USA) was used as a protein standard. Protein concentrations were quantified using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Walterson Biotechnology, Inc., China) [18].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of pH and temperature on degradation activity of the purified enzyme

ce:list-item.ce:para: Optimal pH and temperature: The optimal pH range of the purified enzyme was 4.0–10.0. The optimal temperature range of the enzyme was 30 °C–70 °C.
Stability of enzyme activity at different pH: The purified enzyme was kept at different pH (4.0–10.0) for 24 h at 37 °C. The activity was tested under standard conditions.

Thermostability of the enzyme: The purified enzyme was dissolved in potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) and kept at 20 °C–80 °C for 1 h. The residual activity was tested under standard conditions. The standard conditions were as described in Section 2.5. The activity of the purified enzyme tested under standard conditions was considered to be 100%.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Activities of purified PBS depolymerase for various substrates
ce:section.ce:para: The purified enzyme was transferred into poly(lactic acid) (PLA) emulsion (0.1%, w/v), PHB emulsion (0.1%, w/v), and poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) emulsion (0.1%, w/v). The activity of the purified enzyme for PLA, PHB, and PCL was as described in Section 2.6.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of metal ions and chemicals
ce:section.ce:para: Different metal ions (Na+, K+, Mg2+, Ni2+, Cu2+, Fe2+, and Zn2+) and different chemicals (EDTA, β-mercaptoethanol, H2O2, and Tween 20) were added into PBS emulsion. The activity of the purified enzyme after adding metal ions and chemicals was determined. The activity of the purified enzyme under standard conditions was considered to be 100%.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of the hydrolysis products of PBS
ce:section.ce:para: Purified PBS depolymerase was incubated with PBS emulsion (0.2%, w/v) at 50 °C for 30 min. The mixture was filtered, and the degraded products were identified by ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (Waters, USA).

Protein bands that were excised from SDS-PAGE gels were analyzed by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF-MS; 4700 Proteomics Analyzer; Applied Biosystems, USA) and the results were compared with data available on NCBI website.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Isolation and identification of PBS-degrading microorganisms
ce:section.ce:para: Several transparent circles were found on the solid isolation medium after incubation at 30 °C for 5 days. Fusarium sp. FS1301 was selected as it had the highest ratio of clear zone diameter to colony diameter. Fig. 1 shows colonies on the PBS agar plate of Fusarium sp. FS1301.

The internal transcribed spacer sequence of rDNA was determined and uploaded to NCBI (GenBank accession no. KJ789101). The sequence aligned with those of reference strains obtained from NCBI. FS1301 belongs to the genus Fusarium, and exhibits 99% similarity to both Fusarium sp. NRRL 43643 (GenBank accession no. JN235259) and the Fusarium solani isolate BR03 (GenBank accession no. JX282604).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradability of the PBS-degrading strain Fusarium sp. FS1301
ce:section.ce:para: Fig 2 a shows that Fusarium sp. FS1301 produced clear zones on the PBS agar plate. PBS emulsion became clear (Fig. 2b) after addition of the culture supernatant, indicating that the culture supernatant may contain PBS depolymerase.

Fig 3 shows the weight loss and degradation rate of PBS films along with incubation time. In the first three days, weight loss and degradation rate were slow, as the strain needed to adapt to the new environment. After the third day, both weight loss and degradation rate increased quickly, which indicated that PBS was degraded and Fusarium sp. FS1301 used PBS as its carbon source [14,19]. Aside from the characteristics of the degrading strain, another reason for acceleration of degradation of PBS films was increase in the surface area of PBS films, as indicated by SEM results.

Fig 4 shows the surface morphology of degraded PBS films. Fusarium sp. FS1301 adhered to the surface of films, producing a rough surface of PBS films after 3 days (Fig. 4b). The filaments of Fusarium sp. FS1301 stretched into the films and caused significant damage, as indicated by the many small holes seen by SEM (Fig. 4c). Over time, the surface of PBS films became rougher and the holes became larger.

The effects of biodegradation on the thermal properties of PBS were investigated using DSC (Fig. 5 a). DSC clearly showed two peaks because of the presence of two different types of crystalline lamella in PBS [6,20]. The melting point of pure PBS was approximately 98 °C. After 24 days of degradation, a decreasing trend in the melting point of PBS was observed, but the change was not statistically significant. Furthermore, crystallinity of PBS films, calculated based on the theoretical ΔH° values of PBS (110.5 J g−1) [21], decreased from 43.25% to 27.05% with extension of degradation time (Fig. 5b).

Next, TGA was used to analyze thermal stability of PBS films. Results under different degradation times are shown in Fig 6 . The decomposition temperature decreased with progression of the degradation process, suggesting that the polymer chains of PBS were damaged by extracellular enzymes from Fusarium sp. FS1301.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of temperature and pH on degradation by PBS depolymerase
ce:section.ce:para: The optimal temperature for the purified enzyme was 50 °C. At 60 °C, the activity of the purified enzyme decreased rapidly (Fig. 8 ). Thermostability of the purified enzyme ranged from 20 °C to 50 °C. At 50 °C, the activity was about 60%. The optimal pH for the purified enzyme was pH 8.0, and the enzyme exhibited high activity from pH 5.0 to 9.0.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Substrate specificity and effect of various metal irons and chemicals on the purified enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: Addition of the purified enzyme had no effect on PLA and PHB emulsions. However, the PCL emulsion became clear after the purified enzyme was added. The effects of various metal ions and chemicals on the purified enzyme are shown in Table 2 . Na+ and K+ increased the activity of the enzyme, Mg2+ had no significant effect on PBS depolymerase activity, and Zn2+ significantly inhibited polymerase activity.

EDTA significantly inhibited the activity of PBS depolymerase, indicating dependence of the active site of the enzyme on existing metal ion. β-Mercaptoethanol broke the disulfide bonds in PBS depolymerase and dramatically decreased the activity of the enzyme. Furthermore, 5 M H2O2 and 1% (v/v) Tween 20 inhibited enzyme activity by 30% and 25%, respectively.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of degradation products of the enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 9 shows the degradation products of PBS emulsion formed upon addition of the purified enzyme. Four new oligomer peaks corresponding to 1, 4-succinate (peak at m/z 116.8), succinate–butanediol (peak at m/z 188.9), succinate–butanediol–succinate (peak at m/z 289.0), and succinate–butanediol–succinate–butanediol (peak at m/z 361.1) were found. However, 1,4-butanediol and butanediol–succinate–butanediol, both of which we expected to be present, were not found in the hydrolysate.
PBS depolymerase was purified and analyzed by MALDI-TOF-MS. The deduced amino acid sequence showed 100% similarity to cutinase (GI2493916).

In the present work, Fusarium sp. FS1301, a PBS-degrading strain, was isolated and its degrading effect on PBS films was characterized. Fusarium sp. FS1301 caused greater weight loss (80%, w/w) of PBS films after 21 days, compared to 60% (w/w) weight loss of PBS films caused by P. antarctica in 6 weeks [12]. The fastest degradation rate of Fusarium sp. FS1301 (37.1 μg cm−2 h−1) observed in our study was also much higher than that of the PBS-degrading fungi A. fumigatus (10.5 μg cm−2 h−1), which was previously isolated by Ishii et al. [10]. SEM micrographs of PBS films degraded by Fusarium sp. FS1301 indicated absence of deep holes. This is different from the case of PHB films degraded by Pseudomonas mendocina DS04-T [22], in which deep holes were found after 48 h of degradation. The surface of PBS films degraded by Fusarium sp. FS1301 were found to contain some big and shallow pits. In general, along with extension of degradation time, crystallinity of the polymer films increased. Abe et al. [23] proposed that this was caused by the non-crystalline part of PHB being degraded first, followed by degradation of the crystalline part. However, in our work, DSC analysis revealed that PBS crystallinity decreased with extension of degradation time. This indicated that Fusarium sp. FS1301 degraded both the amorphous and crystalline parts of PBS, causing damage to the crystalline structure. Furthermore, results of TGA showed that the weight loss transition temperature shifted from high to low with increase in degradation time. This was caused by disintegration of polymer chains in PBS films as degradation progressed. Scission of polymer chains caused the overall molecular weight of the polymer to decrease, resulting in broader molecular weight distribution, which led to further lowering of the degradation temperature. Thus, our TGA results are similar to changes in PCL [19] or PHB [22] biodegradation reported previously.

PBS depolymerase from Fusarium sp. FS1301 was also purified and characterized in this study. The molecular mass of PBS depolymerase was found to be similar to that of the PBS degrading enzyme (21.6 kDa) from A. oryzae, which was identified as cutinase [14]. The specific activity of the PBS degrading enzyme from A. oryzae was determined to be 0.42U/mg, which is lower than that of the purified enzyme from Fusarium sp. FS1301 as shown in Table 1. Analysis of substrate specificity revealed that besides PBS, the depolymerase could also degrade PCL, but not PHB and PLA. This is different from the property of the enzyme from A. oryzae which can degrade both PBS and PLA [14].

The deduced amino acid sequence of the depolymerase showed 100% similarity to that of cutinase from F. solani (GI2493916). In general, F. solani is used as a source of cutinase, which is used to degrade cutin in some applications [24,25]. However, there have been only few reports suggesting the ability of F. solani to degrade PBS or other biodegradable plastics to date. Abe et al. found that F. solani degraded 2.8% of PBS in the soil environment and assumed the depolymerase was cutinase but provided no direct evidence [11]. Another study reported that F. solani could degrade PCL, and that its depolymerase could be a type of cutinase [26]. In this work, we identified a highly potent PBS-degrading strain that can also produce cutinase with PBS-degrading activity.

Fusarium sp. FS1301, a PBS-degrading strain, exhibits good PBS degradability. Studies of its degradation activity are important for understanding degradation mechanisms and their use in managing polymer wastes. The PBS depolymerase in Fusarium sp. FS1301 is identical to a cutinase in F. solani. Our findings suggest that F. solani and its cutinase may be useful alternatives for degradation of polymer wastes.
